lessonTitle: Transcription Factors and Regulatory Elements: Promoters, Enhancers and the lac Operon

blocks.text: Move a bacterium from a glucose broth to a lactose broth and, for a few minutes, it cannot use the new sugar. Then, within minutes, enzymes to digest lactose appear in the cell, and when the lactose is gone they disappear again. How does a cell with no brain sense its environment and switch genes on and off?

blocks.markdown: Every cell in the body carries the same genome, yet a neuron, a red cell precursor and a hepatocyte use different genes. Most control of gene expression occurs at the level of **transcription initiation**. It depends on **cis-acting regulatory elements**, DNA sequences located on the same DNA molecule as the gene they control, and **trans-acting factors**, diffusible proteins (mainly transcription factors) that bind to those sequences.

rows: Immediately around the transcription start site (for example TATA box about 25-30 bp upstream)
Binding site for general transcription factors and RNA polymerase II; sets the start site
Binding sites for gene-specific transcription factors that modulate the basal level
Can be thousands to hundreds of thousands of base pairs away, upstream, downstream or within an intron
Binds activators; increases transcription; works in either orientation, acting by looping of DNA to contact the promoter
blocks.caption: Cis-acting regulatory elements in eukaryotes.

blocks.title: Transcription factor
blocks.text: A transcription factor is a protein that binds to specific DNA sequences and increases (activator) or decreases (repressor) the rate of transcription. Most have a DNA-binding domain (such as a zinc finger, helix-turn-helix, homeodomain or leucine zipper) and a separate domain that activates or represses transcription by interacting with other proteins.

blocks.markdown: **How enhancers and activators work.** An activator bound at an enhancer interacts, through the **Mediator** complex and by looping of the intervening DNA, with the general transcription factors and RNA polymerase II at the promoter, increasing the probability of initiation. Activators also recruit chromatin-modifying enzymes such as histone acetyltransferases that open chromatin. Repressors do the opposite. Because genes have many binding sites, **combinatorial control** operates: a gene is expressed only when the right *combination* of factors is present, so a small number of factors can specify many cell types, and the same factor can regulate different genes in different cells. The positions of enhancers explain how genes can be expressed at the right time and place in development; for example, a limb-specific enhancer controls expression of the Sonic hedgehog gene.

**The lac operon: a model of inducible regulation in prokaryotes.** In bacteria, genes with related functions are often clustered into an **operon**, transcribed together as one polycistronic mRNA under a single promoter. The *lac* operon of *E. coli* contains three structural genes: *lacZ* (beta-galactosidase, which splits lactose into glucose and galactose and makes allolactose), *lacY* (lactose permease, which transports lactose into the cell) and *lacA* (a transacetylase). Upstream lie the **promoter** and the **operator**, a short DNA sequence where the repressor binds. A separate gene, *lacI*, which is expressed constantly, encodes the **lac repressor**.

blocks.title: Negative control by the lac repressor
blocks.text: Without lactose, the lac repressor binds the operator and physically blocks RNA polymerase, so the operon is off. When lactose is present, a small amount is converted to allolactose, the inducer, which binds to the repressor and changes its shape so that it releases the operator, allowing RNA polymerase to transcribe lacZYA. The operon is therefore inducible: the substrate induces the enzymes that metabolise it.

blocks.markdown: **Positive control by CAP and catabolite repression.** Even with lactose present, transcription is only strong when glucose is absent. When glucose is low, intracellular cyclic AMP (cAMP) rises and binds the **catabolite activator protein (CAP)**; the cAMP-CAP complex binds near the promoter and enhances RNA polymerase binding. When glucose is abundant, cAMP is low, CAP does not bind, and expression stays low even if lactose is present. The cell thus switches on the lac genes strongly only when lactose is available *and* glucose, the preferred fuel, is scarce.

blocks.title: Predicting the effect of a mutation in lacI
blocks.prompt: A mutant E. coli has a deletion that removes a functional lac repressor (lacI-) but has a normal lacZYA and operator. Predict beta-galactosidase production in a medium with no lactose and no glucose, and explain.

steps.text: Normally, without lactose, the repressor binds the operator and blocks transcription. Here the repressor is absent.
No repressor means nothing blocks RNA polymerase. Glucose is absent, so cAMP-CAP is bound and promotes transcription.
The operon is therefore transcribed even without lactose: expression is constitutive (not dependent on the inducer).

blocks.answer: High beta-galactosidase production without lactose (constitutive expression).

blocks.title: Fold induction
blocks.prompt: An E. coli culture without lactose has beta-galactosidase activity of 4 units per milligram of protein; after lactose is added (and glucose is absent), activity is 3,200 units per milligram. Calculate the fold induction.

steps.text: Fold induction is induced activity divided by uninduced activity.
Interpret the result: the enzyme level rose 800 times, which is far above basal expression and shows strong induction.

blocks.markdown: **Diseases of regulatory sequences.** Because regulatory DNA controls when, where and how much a gene is expressed, mutations in it can cause disease without changing the protein sequence. Examples: **point mutations in the promoter** (including the TATA box) of the beta-globin gene reduce transcription and cause a mild form of **beta-thalassaemia**; **point mutations in a distant limb enhancer of the Sonic hedgehog gene** (the ZRS, which lies within an intron of a neighbouring gene) cause ectopic SHH expression in the limb bud and **preaxial polydactyly**; and variants in an enhancer upstream of the lactase gene determine whether lactase continues to be made into adulthood (lactase persistence). Mutations in transcription factors themselves also cause developmental disease.

items: Promoters bind general factors and RNA polymerase II; enhancers act at a distance by DNA looping.
Transcription factors have DNA-binding and effector domains; combinations of factors control each gene.
lac operon: repressor on the operator blocks transcription; allolactose releases it; cAMP-CAP boosts transcription when glucose is low.
Regulatory mutations can cause disease without altering the protein sequence.

blocks.title: Cis versus trans
blocks.text: A mutation in an operator or enhancer acts only on the DNA molecule that carries it (cis-acting). A mutation in a gene encoding a repressor or activator affects genes on all DNA molecules in the cell (trans-acting).

points: Promoters, enhancers and silencers are cis-acting sequences that bind transcription factors; enhancers act at a distance through DNA looping and combinations of factors control each gene.
In the lac operon the repressor blocks transcription until allolactose releases it, and cAMP-CAP increases transcription when glucose is low.
Mutations in promoters and enhancers, such as those of beta-globin and the Sonic hedgehog limb enhancer, cause disease by altering the level or pattern of expression.

questions.stem: Which description best fits an enhancer?

options.text: A DNA sequence that binds activators and can act at a distance from the promoter, in either orientation
The site at which RNA polymerase begins transcription
A protein that unwinds DNA at the replication fork
A sequence that must lie immediately upstream of the start site to work

questions.correctOptionText: A DNA sequence that binds activators and can act at a distance from the promoter, in either orientation

distractorRationale.a: Correct: enhancers act at a distance, independently of orientation.
distractorRationale.b: This describes the promoter or transcription start site.
distractorRationale.d: Enhancers do not need to lie next to the start site.

questions.explanation: Enhancers bind activator proteins and loop DNA to contact the promoter and general transcription factors. They work at long distances and in either orientation, unlike the core promoter.

questions.stem: In the lac operon, what is the effect of allolactose binding to the lac repressor?

options.text: The repressor changes shape and leaves the operator, allowing transcription
The repressor binds more tightly to the operator
The repressor is degraded and not resynthesised
The repressor binds to RNA polymerase and activates it

questions.correctOptionText: The repressor changes shape and leaves the operator, allowing transcription

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the inducer causes an allosteric change that releases the repressor.
distractorRationale.b: Allolactose reduces, not increases, binding to the operator.
distractorRationale.c: The repressor is not degraded; it is reversibly inactivated.
distractorRationale.d: The repressor acts at the operator, not on RNA polymerase.

questions.explanation: Allolactose, the inducer, binds the repressor and causes an allosteric change that reduces its affinity for the operator. RNA polymerase can then transcribe lacZYA.

questions.stem: E. coli cells are grown in a medium containing both glucose and lactose. Which of the following correctly describes the state of the lac operon?

options.text: Repressor released from the operator but cAMP-CAP not bound, so expression is low
Repressor bound to the operator and cAMP-CAP bound, so expression is high
Repressor bound to the operator, so expression is zero
Repressor released and cAMP-CAP bound, so expression is maximal

questions.correctOptionText: Repressor released from the operator but cAMP-CAP not bound, so expression is low

distractorRationale.a: Correct: lactose inactivates the repressor, but high glucose means low cAMP so CAP does not boost transcription.
distractorRationale.b: With lactose present the repressor is not bound.
distractorRationale.c: Lactose is present, so the repressor is released.
distractorRationale.d: High glucose lowers cAMP, so CAP is not bound.

questions.explanation: Lactose (via allolactose) relieves repression, but glucose keeps cAMP low so CAP does not enhance transcription. The result is a low level of expression until glucose is used up.

questions.stem: A mutant E. coli carries a lacI mutation that produces a repressor unable to bind allolactose but still able to bind the operator. What is the expected phenotype?

options.text: The operon is never induced, even when lactose is present and glucose absent
The operon is expressed constitutively
The operon is induced normally
The operon is expressed only in the presence of glucose

questions.correctOptionText: The operon is never induced, even when lactose is present and glucose absent

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the repressor stays on the operator whatever the inducer level.
distractorRationale.b: Constitutive expression would need a repressor that cannot bind the operator, or an operator mutation.
distractorRationale.c: Induction requires the repressor to respond to allolactose.

questions.explanation: If the repressor cannot be inactivated by the inducer, it remains on the operator and blocks transcription at all times. This is the opposite of the constitutive phenotype of a repressor that cannot bind the operator.

questions.stem: A child is born with an extra thumb on each hand (preaxial polydactyly). Sequencing shows normal protein-coding sequence of the Sonic hedgehog gene but a point mutation in a limb-specific regulatory element located far from the gene. Which mechanism best explains the finding?

options.text: The mutated enhancer drives inappropriate expression of the gene in the limb bud
The mutation changes the amino acid sequence of the protein
The mutation deletes the gene from the limb cells
The mutation causes non-disjunction in meiosis

questions.correctOptionText: The mutated enhancer drives inappropriate expression of the gene in the limb bud

distractorRationale.a: Correct: a regulatory mutation changes where or when the gene is expressed without altering the protein.
distractorRationale.c: The gene is intact and is expressed in the wrong place.
distractorRationale.d: Non-disjunction changes chromosome number, not a single regulatory element.

questions.explanation: Enhancer mutations can alter the spatial or temporal pattern of expression while leaving the protein unchanged. Ectopic expression of Sonic hedgehog in the anterior limb bud leads to extra digits.

questions.stem: In a bacterial culture grown without lactose, beta-galactosidase activity is 6 units per milligram of protein. After addition of lactose, with glucose absent, the activity rises to 4,500 units per milligram. What is the fold induction? Give a ratio.
questions.explanation: Fold induction is induced activity divided by uninduced activity: 4500 / 6 = 750. This large change illustrates the dynamic range of regulation by the repressor and CAP.

questions.stem: The polycistronic lacZYA mRNA of E. coli is about 5,000 nucleotides long. If RNA polymerase transcribes at an average of 50 nucleotides per second, how long does it take to transcribe the operon? Give your answer in seconds.
questions.explanation: Time equals length divided by rate: 5000 nt / 50 nt per second = 100 seconds. The three genes are transcribed as a single polycistronic mRNA from one promoter.

questions.stem: True or false: An enhancer must be located immediately adjacent to the promoter of its target gene and in the correct orientation to function.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Enhancers can act over long distances, upstream, downstream or within introns, and in either orientation, by looping of DNA to contact the promoter.

questions.stem: Describe how promoters, enhancers and transcription factors cooperate to control the expression of a eukaryotic gene, and explain how combinatorial control allows different cell types to express different genes.
markingGuide: Promoter: binding site for general transcription factors and RNA polymerase II at the start site (e.g. TATA box).
Enhancers: distal, orientation-independent sites bound by activators that loop to the promoter, using Mediator, and recruit chromatin modifiers.
Transcription factors: DNA-binding domain and regulatory (activation or repression) domain; activators and repressors.
Combinatorial control: a gene needs the right combination of factors, so a limited set of factors specifies many expression patterns and cell types.
questions.explanation: Gene-specific factors bind enhancers and promoter-proximal elements and communicate with the basal machinery, and the combination present in each cell determines which genes are on.

questions.stem: Explain how the lac operon is regulated in the four combinations of glucose present or absent and lactose present or absent, naming the repressor, the inducer and the role of cAMP-CAP. Then give one example of human disease caused by a mutation in a regulatory sequence.
markingGuide: No lactose: repressor (lacI product) binds the operator and blocks RNA polymerase; operon off regardless of glucose.
Lactose present: allolactose (inducer) binds the repressor, which releases the operator.
Glucose present: low cAMP, CAP not bound, so transcription is low even with lactose.
Glucose absent with lactose: high cAMP, cAMP-CAP bound near promoter, high expression.
Disease example of regulatory mutation: beta-globin promoter mutation causing beta-thalassaemia, or ZRS enhancer mutation causing preaxial polydactyly.
questions.explanation: The lac operon integrates negative control (repressor) with positive control (cAMP-CAP) so it is strongly on only when lactose is present and glucose is scarce. Regulatory mutations in humans change the level or pattern of expression without changing the protein.
